blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A `Shipment` class declares no constructors, and the order service's mapper builds shipments by calling its no-argument constructor through reflection. A developer adds `Shipment(String trackingCode)` for a new screen and changes nothing else. What happens when the team builds and deploys?

options.text: The build passes and the first mapping throws NoSuchMethodException, since the added constructor took the place of the one Java had supplied
options.says: the default constructor exists only while a class declares none; reflection finds out at run time

options.text: The build passes and the first mapping returns a Shipment with a null trackingCode, since Java keeps the no-argument constructor it supplied beside the declared one
options.says: declaring any constructor removes the default one

options.text: The build fails with 'cannot find symbol' at the mapper's call, since javac checks which constructors a reflective lookup can reach
options.says: javac doesn't check which constructor a reflective lookup asks for; it fails only when it runs

options.text: The build fails with 'constructor already defined' at the new constructor, since Java had already supplied one for the class
options.says: the supplied constructor takes no arguments and disappears once one is declared; nothing clashes

origin.section: Declaring Any Constructor Takes Away the Default One

questions.stem: `Range(int low, int high)` refuses `low > high`. On Java 21 a colleague adds `Range(String text) { String[] p = text.split("-"); this(Integer.parseInt(p[0]), Integer.parseInt(p[1])); }` so that "10-20" can be read from a file. What do you tell them?

options.text: It doesn't compile; assign low and high in this constructor instead, since the check in the two-int constructor still runs for every Range
options.says: a constructor that assigns its own fields never runs the other constructor's check

options.text: It doesn't compile; compute the two numbers with static methods inside the this(...) call, since that call has to come first
options.says: this(...) must be the first statement, and static methods in its arguments can compute what it needs

options.text: It compiles and runs the check, since a this(...) call may come anywhere as long as it comes before the fields are used
options.says: on Java 21 javac rejects any statement before this(...)

options.text: It compiles and skips the check, since a this(...) call after a statement runs as an ordinary method call
options.says: javac rejects it with 'call to this must be first statement in constructor', so nothing runs

origin.section: Overloaded Constructors Chain with this(...) to One That Checks and Assigns

questions.stem: A `Session` constructor first calls `registry.add(this)`, then assigns its final `user` field, then checks a token and throws `IllegalStateException` because the token expired. The caller catches the exception and, on the same thread, looks in the registry. What does the registry hold for that session?

options.text: Nothing, since the token check threw before the constructor finished, and the add was undone with it
options.says: nothing is undone: the registry got the reference before the throw and keeps it

options.text: Nothing, since add(this) ran while the constructor was still running, and the registry gets the object only when it returns
options.says: add(this) stores the reference at once; the registry holds it while the constructor goes on

options.text: A Session with its user set, since add(this) ran before the token check threw
options.says: the registry got a reference before the throw; the assignments before the throw stay done

options.text: A Session with its user null, since add(this) ran before the user was assigned, and the registry kept that state
options.says: the registry holds a reference, not a snapshot; the user assigned after the add is visible through it

origin.section: A Constructor That Hands Out this Lets Others Use a Half-Built Object

questions.stem: A library's `Region` has a private constructor and a factory `Region.of(String code)`, documented as returning the region with that code. Your service compares regions with `if (region == Region.of("eu-west"))`. Is that comparison sound?

options.text: Yes, since a factory documented to return the region for a code returns the one object kept for that code
options.says: returning a region with that code says nothing about identity; only an explicit promise, such as Currency's, does

options.text: Yes, since the private constructor leaves `of` as the only source of regions, so each code gets one object
options.says: a private constructor only routes callers through the factory; whether it reuses objects is up to the factory

options.text: No, since the documentation of `of` promises the region for a code, not the same object on every call
options.says: rely on identity only where the javadoc promises it, as Currency's does

options.text: No, since `==` compares two regions' codes only while the library holds those regions in a cache of its own
options.says: == compares references, always; what the check depends on is whether of returns the same object

origin.section: A Static Factory Can Name, Reuse or Choose the Class of What It Returns

concepts: A static factory can have a name, return an existing object or a subclass, while new always makes a new object of the named class; callers rely on identity or class only where documented.
On Java 21 a this(...) or super(...) call must be the first statement and its arguments can't read instance fields; arguments are computed by static methods inside the call.
